video_title: Why Too Much Efficiency Makes Us Fragile with Olivier Hamant | TGS 230
gist: French plant biologist Olivier Hamant argues with Nate Hagens that the root cause of civilizational fragility is not oil, selfishness or individualism but a cultural tropism toward performance (efficacy + efficiency), and that biology instead selects for robustness — stability and viability across fluctuations. He lays out a testable framework (four determinants plus a stress test), argues the world is leaving 'the era of the mean' for 'the era of the standard deviation,' and gives concrete adoption evidence: agroecology acreage rising annually in Europe for 20 years, ~700 people in Francophone robustness communities, cities (Lyon, Rennes) adding robustness to decision criteria, and a 6,000-CEO French association switching from global performance to robustness this year.

themes.theme: Robustness vs. performance: the core trade-off

insights.claim: Olivier Hamant defines performance as the sum of efficacy (reaching an objective) and efficiency (with the least means), and robustness as the capacity of a system to stay stable and viable despite fluctuations — and insists the two are in direct trade-off at every scale and timeframe.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Gives an operational vocabulary for scoring any asset, firm or supply chain: optimized-for-throughput systems are structurally short volatility, and the trade-off means efficiency gains are not free.
insights.quote: the capacity of a system to be stable and viable despite fluctuations

insights.claim: Living systems put robustness before performance while 21st-century human societies inverted that ordering, which Hamant says places modern civilization in Charles Perrow's 'normal accident' regime where high complexity plus high interdependence makes failure unavoidable.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Frames globalized, tightly-coupled systems (supply chains, AI stacks) as carrying an embedded failure probability that no amount of further optimization reduces.
insights.quote: globalizations, AI, I mean, all this is designed to fail

insights.claim: Hamant deliberately abandoned the word 'resilience' and rejects Nassim Taleb's 'anti-fragile' because both describe trajectories that require falling first; robustness instead means enlarging the space of viability so you never fall, and he calls the Japanese post-Fukushima resilience plan of exposing people to radiation a bad Darwinian reading.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: A sharper distinction than the resilience language most ESG and risk frameworks use: robustness is a state space to be widened ex ante, not a recovery curve measured ex post.
insights.quote: resilience is you fall and then you bounce back. Robustness, it's you create the conditions in which you don't fall.

insights.claim: Hamant argues Darwin's Origin of Species is a claim for selection of the most adaptable rather than the most adapted, so evolution does not select the most efficient organism — the shark is robust but not efficient, while highly specialized orchids co-evolved with a single insect are the ones most likely to disappear.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Directly contradicts the economic intuition that competitive selection produces efficiency; the analogue is that hyper-specialized single-customer or single-input businesses are the natural extinction candidates.
insights.quote: Evolution does not select the most efficient. Evolution selects the most robust

insights.claim: Performance is legitimate only at the peak of a crisis — a fireman fighting a fire, a lion hunting — but the lion sleeps sixteen to twenty hours a day, whereas modern humans are pushed into performance mode roughly ninety percent of waking time.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant and Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Suggests an economy calibrated to permanent crisis-mode allocation; the investable inverse is anything that monetizes slack, downtime and multi-use capacity rather than utilization rates.
insights.quote: the lion that is hunting is performant, but the lion is sleeping sixteen to twenty hours every day

insights.claim: Hamant names the root cause of ecological and social overshoot as the cultural tropism toward performance — explicitly not selfishness, not individualism, and not even oil — and says it produces a planetary burnout affecting humans, public services and ecosystems alike.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Reframes the overshoot debate away from energy substitution toward institutional objective functions — meaning fixing energy supply alone would not fix the underlying driver.
insights.quote: It's not s- selfishness, it's not, individualism, it's not even oil.

insights.claim: Diversity functions as heterogeneous redundancy and acts as a shield against pathogens: a wheat monoculture is homogeneous enough to select for the pathogen that attacks it, and Hamant explicitly maps the same logic onto cyberattacks that target the dominant software.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: A biological argument for why dominant-platform market share is itself a risk factor — monoculture concentration in software or seeds converts efficiency into a single point of systemic failure.
insights.quote: It's the same for informatics, by the way, the cyber attacks, they attack the dominant software, right?

insights.claim: What survives 21st-century bottlenecks will be heterogeneous collective populations rather than individual super-species, because engineering one drought- and frost-resistant tree and planting it as a monoculture simply attracts a pathogen that destroys the forest.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: A direct caution against climate-adaptation investment theses built on single engineered cultivars or single-technology fixes.
insights.quote: what will resist is collective robustness, so a collection of different species that will mutually help each other

themes.theme: Resource abundance as the fragility engine

insights.claim: Hamant's biological law of abundance: place any living being in an ecological niche with abundant resources and it turns into a parasite — an optimized extracting machine that loses its other capacities — which is exactly what happened to humans once they learned to mine vertically for ancient sunlight.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Predicts that resource-rich environments systematically destroy optionality, so windfall-driven business models should be assumed to have shed capabilities they will need later.
insights.quote: then you turn into a parasite. So that means that you optimize yourself.

insights.claim: The same organism placed in a scarce, fluctuating niche cooperates rather than competes, and Hamant says symbiosis dominates Earth far more than parasitism — citing the resource-poor ocean, where network analyses of species interactions show cooperation rather than the shark-and-danger image.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Implies energy and materials decline should mechanically push economies toward cooperative, shared-asset structures rather than pure Hobbesian competition.

insights.claim: The three years from 1945 to 1948 produced a burst of robustness-building institutions — social security, human rights, the IUCN — created because societies had just experienced extreme fluctuations, but after 1948 the return of even more abundant oil reversed the trend back toward performance.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Historical evidence that institution-building for robustness follows trauma within a narrow window and decays under renewed energy abundance — a timing heuristic for policy-driven investment cycles.

insights.claim: Hamant says there was no first-order difference between the US and USSR in the 1960s — both were extractivist economies pumping oil and mining minerals — and points out salary inequality fell from the 1950s to the 1970s and then rose after the 1970s oil shocks in both countries, meaning the driver is resource abundance rather than the economic model.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: If inequality tracks resource abundance rather than capitalism versus communism, then distributional forecasts should be indexed to energy and materials availability, not political regime.
insights.quote: there's no difference between the US and USSR in the '60s. These are two extractivist economy.

insights.claim: Adding control decreases security rather than increasing it: Hamant's example is that double authentication lowers a user's own vigilance, which makes a fraudulent banker more credible, and he generalizes that optimization makes systems more fragile in ways participants cannot see.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: A counterintuitive risk model for security and compliance spending: layered controls can transfer risk into the least-monitored human layer instead of removing it.
insights.quote: when we increase the level of control, actually we increase the level of insecurity

insights.claim: Hamant describes humanity as in 'evolutive mismatch' — still carrying the culture of abundance and performance after the underlying world has changed — and points to physical evidence: the jaw has shrunk from eating tenderer food, and dental cavities and vitamin deficiencies both trace to the narrower diet that agriculture introduced.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Argues the cultural lag, not the physical constraint, is the binding problem — so the mispricing is in beliefs and institutions rather than in resources themselves.
insights.quote: we are exactly in what we call, what we biologists call evolutive mismatch

themes.theme: The era of the standard deviation

insights.claim: Hamant says the first line of every scientific report on the socioecological question is that we are leaving the era of the mean and entering the era of the standard deviation, and that climate, pollution and energy are secondary problems downstream of ecological overshoot destroying the buffers that made life predictable.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: The single most portable trade idea in the conversation: systematically long variance and optionality, short mean-reversion assumptions embedded in infrastructure, insurance and agricultural models.
insights.quote: we are leaving the era of the mean and we are entering the era of the standard deviation

insights.claim: Designing on standard deviations rather than means changes the physical solution: someone living by the sea who thinks in means builds a dike against slow sea-level rise, while someone thinking in deviations builds an amphibious habitat that can withstand water coming in and going out because submersion could come tomorrow.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Concrete screen for climate-adaptation capital: dike-type projects are mean-based bets likely to be stranded, amphibious and relocatable designs price the tail.
insights.quote: You're going to make an habitat that can withstand this water coming in, so it's gonna be more amphibious

insights.claim: Hamant argues risk only looks like danger because everything has been over-optimized, and that the fix is to 're-enchant risk' by building economic and social systems on fluctuations so that when shocks arrive they are welcome rather than frightening — the posture of a jazz musician rather than a score-reading performer.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Reframes volatility tolerance as a designable organizational property rather than a psychological trait — relevant to how firms structure buffers and decision rights.
insights.quote: You have to re-enchant risk.

insights.claim: Multi-use and dismantlable design is the built-environment expression of robustness: an efficient house optimizes every room and builds in the furniture, while a robust house has movable walls and can be taken apart and rebuilt elsewhere when it needs to become a hospital or house more people.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Points at reconfigurable and demountable building stock as the asset class that holds value in a high-variance regime, versus purpose-built single-use property.
insights.quote: if you want to be robust, it has to be multi-use

insights.claim: COVID proved cities still hold latent multi-use capacity — sidewalks became waiting rooms and plazas became vaccination centres — and Hamant says the priority now is to see, cherish, preserve and expand those spaces before they are re-optimized away.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Municipal zoning and public-space policy becomes a robustness variable, and the window to lock in flexible-use rules is closing as cities re-optimize.

insights.claim: Hamant rejects sobriety as a policy input, arguing that efficiency-driven sobriety triggers the rebound effect — more fuel-efficient planes made low-cost flights and ultra-fast fashion possible and exhausted resources — so sobriety should be the output of robustness rather than an imposed constraint.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Predicts efficiency-mandate policy (fuel standards, appliance efficiency) fails to cut absolute throughput, so demand forecasts built on efficiency gains understate consumption.
insights.quote: sobriety is, actually, it's a nice word, but it shouldn't be the cause. It shouldn't be the constraint.

insights.claim: Nate Hagens argues humans do not need base load because humans are base load — historically napping like a lion when it rained and working when it was sunny and windy — implying the cultural demand for constant-availability power is itself an artifact of the performance regime.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Challenges the assumption underpinning firm-capacity and storage investment theses: demand-side temporal flexibility is an unpriced substitute for base load generation.
insights.quote: Humans don't need base load. We are base load

insights.claim: Hamant says multiple reports show a switch to agroecology could feed eight billion people with no problem, and defines agroecology as treating the agrosystem as an ecosystem — replacing fertilizer, pesticides and irrigation with in-field biodiversity that supplies nutrients, pathogen resistance and soil water retention.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: If credible, this is a demand-destruction thesis for synthetic nitrogen, crop protection chemicals and irrigation equipment over a multi-decade horizon.
insights.quote: If we could switch to agroecology, you can feed eight billion people, no problem.

insights.claim: The surface area under agroecology in Europe has increased every year for the past 20 years, and Hamant attributes it to economics rather than ideology: new farmers can no longer afford to start with intensive agriculture because it is too expensive, so they start with agroecology directly.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Input-cost inflation, not subsidy or sentiment, is driving the acreage shift — a structurally durable headwind for input suppliers and a tailwind for low-input agronomy services.
insights.quote: you can't start with intensive agriculture anymore. It's too expensive.

insights.claim: A modern treeless wheat or canola field produces roughly the same total biomass as a savanna, because agriculture globally copied the Fertile Crescent savanna model from Syria and exported it even to places that were forests.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Reframes modern yields as low on a total-biomass basis, opening headroom for agroforestry systems that stack production rather than optimize a single crop.
insights.quote: Actually, it's the, same yield as the savanna.

insights.claim: Agroforestry — putting trees on top of a wheat field — produces substantially more biomass per square meter while protecting the field from rain and maintaining soil structure, which Hamant presents as the upgrade path from the savanna-derived model.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Positions agroforestry as the yield-and-resilience play in land investment, with carbon and water co-benefits that single-crop systems cannot capture.

insights.claim: Hamant concedes the agroecology transition requires far more human labour in the fields and that Western material lifestyles could not be maintained under it, but rejects the framing that it means returning to the Middle Ages — the technology is retained, just made robust, repairable, locally produced and locally repaired.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant and Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: A labour-intensity constraint that would show up as agricultural wage inflation and food cost share increases — and a bull case for repairable, locally serviceable farm equipment.
insights.quote: there would be more people working in the fields. I mean, right now it's crazy. There's almost no- no one

insights.claim: Norman Borlaug's land-sparing theory failed through the rebound effect: raising yields was supposed to prevent deforestation, but higher yields created new needs such as palm oil and soy that increased deforestation instead — Hamant's example that Jevons-type dynamics operate at the biology–economy boundary.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Undercuts intensification-for-conservation arguments used to justify high-input agriculture and precision-ag productivity claims.

insights.claim: The Neoloko bakery bakes bread in a plain mirror-based solar oven in cloudy Normandy by using a slower, less performant yeast that produces bread storable for seven days, which makes the baker independent of oil prices, of Russia invading Ukraine, of inflation, of subsidised competition — and robust enough not to need subsidies at all.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: The clearest worked example that robustness is an economic moat: removing input dependencies raises margin stability more than process efficiency does.
insights.quote: you're so robust that you don't even need the subsidies

insights.claim: Hamant argues AI's truth is correlative, so its attractor is the mean and not the standard deviation — the more AI is used, the more attention concentrates on what is widespread on the internet and the less on what is unusual, which is precisely backwards for a world entering higher fluctuation.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Predicts AI adoption systematically degrades tail-risk perception and creative variance — a strategic argument for preserving non-AI research and heterodox sourcing.
insights.quote: the attractor for an AI is the mean. It's not the standard deviation.

insights.claim: Delegating tasks to AI causes de-learning and competency loss — Hamant cites surgeons as an example and says knowledge is exported to the machine while competence is lost, calling AI a tool to de-learn and become less adaptable.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: A skills-atrophy liability that would first surface in high-stakes professional domains — relevant to malpractice, training costs and workforce continuity risk.
insights.quote: it's, really, it's a tool to de-learn and to be less adaptable

insights.claim: The only design in which AI serves robustness, per Hamant, is deliberately inefficient AI that requires humans to check and verify both before and after, adding new sources, references and serendipity — with the side benefit of lower environmental impact because it is less performant.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: An unusual product spec: intentionally slower, human-gated AI as a differentiated category, cutting against the industry's throughput-and-autonomy roadmap.
insights.quote: We want to make non or very inefficient AI, where humans have to go afterwards to check

insights.claim: Hamant argues competition-driven innovation is confined to the space competitors leave, so it produces only small innovations and gadgets, whereas cooperation expands the innovation space — noting that when evolution produces a new type of leg or wing there is no patent on it.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Directly contests the premise that IP protection maximizes innovation output, with implications for open-source and commons-based R&D valuation.
insights.quote: When we innovate with competition, we restrict the innovation. There's a patent, there's a limit

insights.claim: Nate Hagens notes historical innovation has delivered roughly 1.1% efficiency improvement per year, remarkably consistent over the last 100 years, and Hamant's response is that innovation has been assumed to serve increased performance when it could equally serve increased robustness, health, meaning and the web of life.
insights.speaker: Nate Hagens and Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Sets a quantitative baseline for what efficiency-directed innovation has actually delivered, against which robustness-directed innovation can be compared.
insights.quote: we've innovated 1.1% a year. We've become more efficient over the last 100 years.

insights.claim: France is running 'calls to commons' procurement where companies bidding on projects — Hamant cites mixed car-bike vehicles — must share all their innovations, with outputs placed in the Creative Commons under CC BY-SA share-alike terms.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: A live public-procurement mechanism that strips IP exclusivity from awarded contracts — a real policy risk and opportunity for firms bidding into European mobility programmes.

insights.claim: Hamant gives four determinants for judging whether a policy or project actually increases robustness rather than merely cutting consumption: redundancy (a plan B, C and D), heterogeneity (those plans must be genuinely different, not the same thing twice), a link to living creatures on site, and a deep social, economic and material link to the local territory.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: A four-factor screen usable as a diligence checklist to separate genuine resilience investments from throughput reduction dressed up as adaptation.

insights.claim: The operational tool Hamant recommends is a stress test asking two questions of any strategic decision — is the project robust, and is it serving the robustness of the territory — shocked with extremes such as a tenfold oil price or no internet anywhere on the planet for six months, which immediately maps where the fragilities sit.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: A concrete scenario set well outside standard corporate stress ranges; running it surfaces dependencies that conventional risk models never touch.
insights.quote: oil price, 10 times, higher, there's no more internet for the next six months on the entire planet

insights.claim: Hamant's tactic for a lone robustness advocate in a group of twenty is not to speak louder — that is the performant path and is counterproductive — but to assemble a deliberately heterogeneous active minority of CEOs, homeless people and bakers that activates the silent majority, which he compares to Sun Tzu and to encirclement in Go.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: A specific, testable change-management mechanic for getting robustness criteria adopted in boards, councils and standard-setting bodies.
insights.quote: That's an active minority. The active minority is activating a silent majority

insights.claim: Hamant expects the transition to be bottom-up and local rather than top-down, saying he strongly doubts the president of the USA or the European Commission will suddenly switch to robustness, and he cites flocks of birds where the periphery, not the centre, guides the group's turns.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Directs attention to municipal and regional procurement as the leading indicator of the robustness shift rather than national policy announcements.

insights.claim: Hamant reports concrete adoption: roughly seven hundred people already in Francophone robustness learning communities across France, Belgium and Quebec after only a few months and growing exponentially; the cities of Lyon and Rennes putting robustness into their decision criteria; and Le Centre des Jeunes Dirigeants, some six thousand French CEOs, deciding this year to switch from global performance to robustness.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Hard adoption numbers to track: a 6,000-CEO association changing its stated management objective is a measurable leading indicator for European corporate criteria shifts.
insights.quote: six thousand CEOs, in France who decided this year to switch from global performance to robustness

insights.claim: Hamant's recommended first concrete step for a community is to build a repair café, because it teaches repair skills, creates a social link and constitutes local cooperation — a seed of robustness in the territory.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Cheapest observable proxy for whether a locality is actually shifting: repair infrastructure precedes broader right-to-repair and durable-goods demand.
insights.quote: A good starting point is to, build a repair cafe

insights.claim: Hamant's first personal recommendation is to clean the vocabulary inherited from the 1980s, singling out 'impact' as a military term implying a fast, turnkey solution — and when Hagens raises impact investing, both agree the honest label would be 'transform investing' because real transformation takes time.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant and Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: A direct critique of the impact-investing category's implicit promise of rapid measurable change, pointing toward longer-horizon transformation mandates.
insights.quote: Impact is really a military term, so it's why would you use this word?

insights.claim: Hamant calls Trustpilot an oxymoron because trust cannot be piloted — trust emerges from uncertainty, as it does in jazz — so star-rating systems are tools of control rather than instruments of trust.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Questions the durability of ratings-and-scoring business models as trust infrastructure, particularly in environments where variance rises.
insights.quote: you can't pilot trust. Trust emerges from uncertainty.

insights.claim: Improvisation and free jazz are Hamant's school of robustness: a performance-obsessed musician stops playing when the wind takes the sheet music, while a free jazz player incorporates a neighbour's odd C sharp into the intention — and he explicitly excludes the marching band.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: An operational test for whether an organization is robust: does an unplanned input get absorbed into the output, or does it stop the process?
insights.quote: you live in the world of standard deviation, you do jazz

insights.claim: Hamant argues rational argument cannot pull someone out of the cult of performance and that only a 'bug' — a derailment such as a burnout, a year working in a different country, or the trouble generated by artists — creates the arrest needed to change habits.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Implies persuasion campaigns and data-driven advocacy will underperform disruptive experience — relevant to how transitions actually get adopted.
insights.quote: the only way you can take someone out of the cult is if you create a bug

insights.claim: Hamant cites a recent Science paper following young virtuosos in sports and music which found most went through burnout and never became champions, while today's 20- and 30-year-old champions were diversified generalists as children doing sports, music, chess and play — so his advice to young people is to explore and be a generalist.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Empirical support that early specialization destroys long-run performance — a human-capital argument against narrow skill investment in a high-variance world.
insights.quote: when you look at the current champions, today's champions that are 20, 30 years old, when they were kids, they were not experts.

insights.claim: Hamant flags security as the topic he expects to dominate the upcoming French presidential election and argues it is being designed as control when security should mean serenity, which he calls the opposite of control.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: A named political catalyst with a stated framing fight attached — worth watching for how security spending and surveillance policy gets justified in France.
insights.quote: security is control, and security should be serenity, which is the opposite of control

insights.claim: Hamant's three lessons from non-human organisms are circularity (waste is a gift that re-feeds the system, and humans are the only ones inventing non-circular outputs like nuclear waste), cooperation and symbiosis under scarcity, and robustness built against performance — which he says is really the first and most important.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: The compressed design brief: products that feed ecosystems, cooperative structures, and viability space over throughput — a filter for circular bioeconomy ventures.
insights.quote: circularity is when it's not a problem to waste things 'cause it's a gift

insights.claim: Hamant redefines intelligence in evolutionary terms as the ability to adapt, arguing the most intelligent living beings are the most adaptable and that humans would more accurately be called Homo adaptibilus — while today cleverness is deployed almost entirely in service of efficiency.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant and Nate Hagens
insights.so_what: Reframes the metric for both human and machine intelligence away from optimization speed toward adaptive range — directly relevant to how AI capability is benchmarked.
insights.quote: intelligence is the ability to adapt. It's adaptability

insights.claim: Asked for one magic-wand change, Hamant chooses transforming agriculture to agroecology and permaculture, arguing it would depollute land and water, store far more carbon in soil, begin solving the climate crisis and feed a circular bioeconomy producing sovereignty.
insights.speaker: Olivier Hamant
insights.so_what: Identifies agriculture as the highest-leverage intervention point in his framework, which is where robustness-aligned capital would concentrate first.
insights.quote: Change the agriculture.
